newsitem.title: USA: Prosecution begins closing argument in bomb case.
newsitem.headline: Prosecution begins closing argument in bomb case.

text.p: Timothy McVeigh bombed the federal building in Oklahoma City out of hatred for the U.S. government, believing his attack would inspire an uprising in America, the prosecution at his trial said on Thursday.

In his closing argument, prosecutor Larry Mackey said evidence clearly proved McVeigh was responsible for the April 19, 1995 blast at the Alfred P. Murrah building that killed 168 people and wounded more than 500 others.
"Suddenly many lives were ended, and many, many more were changed forever," Mackey said. "America stood in shock. ... Who could do such a thing?
"Based on the evidence, the answer is clear. Tim McVeigh did it," he said.

He said McVeigh's rage was prompted by the government's 1993 siege at the Branch Davidian compound in Waco, Texas, where some 80 people died. McVeigh hoped his attack would trigger more violence against the government, he said.

"Tim McVeigh was wrong about America. He was wrong about America's response," he said. McVeigh's deed stunned America, he said. "At that time, no one in America would have thought an American would bomb his own people."

McVeigh, 29, faces the death penalty if convicted of federal murder and conspiracy charges. Wearing a blue plaid shirt, khaki pants and his hair in a crewcut, he sat in the crowded courtroom and appeared to be listening intently. His brow was furrowed and he rested his chin on his hand.
Following the prosecution's closing statement, defence attorneys for McVeigh were to deliver their closing piece and jury deliberations were to begin after final instructions from the judge.

The prosecutor told the jury McVeigh was inspired by "The Turner Diaries," a novel about the violent overthrow of the U.S. governemnt by a band of right-wing extremists. But he said McVeigh was not on trial for his right-wing extremist views. "In America, everyone has a right to their beliefs. ... This is a murder case," Mackey said.
He reviewed the government's evidence, reciting alibis allegedly used by McVeigh and co-conspirator Terry Nichols and storage lockers they allegedly rented.
He said McVeigh gathered up the bomb's ingredients, bought a how-to book on building bombs and drove to Oklahoma City to survey his intended target. Nichols is to be tried separately.
"The government has presented a smorgasbord of evidence. You can pick and choose," he said. "You can push away entirely satisfied that the government has proved its case beyond a reasonable doubt."

He also defended the prosecution's star witnesses, Michael and Lori Fortier, who testified that McVeigh told them of the bombing in advance. Defence attorneys portrayed them as an irresponsible couple who lied in hopes of selling their story.
"Tim McVeigh has presented the Fortiers as morally corrupt drug abusers. Not too long ago, they were his friends," Mackey said.

He also described McVeigh's arrest 90 minutes after the blast. "From every corner of America, people responded," he said, pointing to McVeigh to add, "One man, this man, was heading in the oppposite direction, out of town."
McVeigh was stopped by a state trooper who noticed his car was missing a license plate.
